constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette: Arthur Vance was in the sub-basement of the Grand Meridian Hotel, reviewing the winterization logs, when the pressure valve on the third-line boiler room fractured. The initial hiss of escaping solvent had been swallowed by the building’s ventilation, but the acrid, chemical-sweet stench hit him the moment he dropped his clipboard. His recollection offered no single sequence; only jagged, disconnected pieces—a flickering fluorescent tube, the slick grip of a steel ladder, the way his lungs burned in quick, shallow pulls. He tried to turn toward the exit, but his legs felt like dead weight, and the heavy iron door clicked shut behind him, sealing the vapor inside. In that dark, pressurized space, Arthur had come to believe he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He felt the full, suffocating panic of that night even now, though no clear image of the event would ever surface in his mind. Only the smell of burnt sugar and copper would return, unbidden and sharp, whenever his attention drifted toward the past. Over the following weeks, Arthur found himself on guard even inside his own house. The kitchen tiles and the study rugs offered no shelter; he could only relax in the back armchair by the fireplace, the one spot where the windows were painted shut and the air seemed still. At the hotel, his attention sharpened to the acoustics of service corridors. Every unexpected clank of a pipe, every dropped tray in the elevator shaft, sent his pulse rising. He sat rigid in his office while maintenance crews worked below, listening for the particular cadence of heavy boots. He filled the rooms with loud music or turned the television up to maximum volume, layering noise until there was no quiet left to navigate. Even in the din, he sifted through his own thoughts, checking for any sign that he was going crazy, any proof that the exposure had fractured his mind permanently. He stopped taking the service elevator entirely, walking two extra flights of stairs each morning just to put distance between himself and the boiler room. His body felt like an enemy, twitching at shadows, jumping at his own reflection, reacting as though the chemical air still filled the halls he walked through. He could no longer trust his own lungs or his nerves, only that they were lying to him about his safety. The distance he needed grew from miles into chasms. Over months, he delegated the night inspections to his assistant manager, then to someone else entirely, until his own office hours shrank to daylight. His ex-wife’s weekly calls went unanswered for seasons, then years, until the silence between them became as thick as the fumes he had breathed. He told himself he was protecting his staff from his growing irritability, but in truth, he was simply trying to outrun a threat that no longer had a location. He finally walked into the community mental health clinic last Tuesday, his pension paperwork clutched in one hand and a faded maintenance map of the city in the other, pointing to the condemned wing of the hotel. He did not want answers about his lungs. He wanted to know how to stop bracing for a collapse that would never come, and how to sit in a room where he might finally, safely, just listen to a record instead of filling the silence. He feared that if he let his guard down even once, the past would rush back in without warning, but he was hoping, however faintly, that someone might show him how to exist in a space where his body no longer sounded the alarm.
